KEY_FINDINGS: Anaerobic biological treatment system was designed primarily to meet effluent standards for selenium. Pilot study results indicate the system can meet effluent standards although the paper does not provide performance data. Plant installed a packed-bed, fixed-film, anaerobic biological treatment system based on the pilot study results.
MOTIVATION: To treat combined power plant wastewater streams to meet upcoming changes in limits for dissolved trace metals using anaerobic digestion.
WASTE_STREAM: Chloride purge stream [(CPS) (FGD Blowdown)] and landfill leachate streams of power plant wastewater.

AUTHORS: Thomas E. Higgins, Karen Meade, Denis Fink
TITLE: Demonstration Test of Iron Addition to a Flue Gas Desulfurization (FGD) Absorber to Enhance Flue Gas Selenium Removal
ABSTRACT: In forced-oxidation flue gas desulfurization (FGD) systems, a significant portion of selenium is selenate. Currently, the only demonstrated technology for selenate removal from FGD wastewater has been biological treatment. This paper presents data showing that the addition of an iron salt to an FGD results in the absorption of selenite with iron hydroxide before it can be oxidized to selenate, thereby lowering the soluble selenium in the FGD wastewater, and allowing removal of the particulate selenium in solids-removal processes.
KEY_FINDINGS: Iron additions to limestone forced-oxidation systems in an effort to increase adsorption of selenite. Two full-scale studies (2009 and 2011) proved to be inconclusive but the tests were promising in that a low iron dose resulted in selenium concentrations below 1 mg/L. The favorable pH for selenite absorption is 5.5 to 6, which is the typical pH range of FGD scrubber operations.
MOTIVATION: To increase the efficiency of FGD systems by adding iron to remove selenium.

AUTHORS: Antonio O. Lau, Rudy Labban, Sunil Mehta, A. Paul Togna
TITLE: Evaluation of Carbon Sources for the Anaerobic Treatment of Flue Gas Desulfurization (FGD) Wastewaters for Heavy Metals Removal
ABSTRACT: In support of a planned full-scale wastewater treatment plant expansion, an evaluation of carbon sources was conducted to find a suitable material that could be used in the anaerobic treatment of flue gas desulfurization (FGD) wastewaters for the biological removal of heavy metals, such as selenium, chromium, vanadium, etc. The major criteria used to evaluate the carbon sources were: (1) heavy metals removal performance, (2) cost-effectiveness, and (3) ease of use of the chemical in full-scale operations. Laboratory-scale studies were conducted using dissolved sugar (sucrose) and a commercial proprietary liquid carbon source (MicroCg™). These carbon sources were fed into a laboratory-scale patented biological anaerobic wastewater treatment system (iBIO®) to test their performance. The biological reactor system used suspended growth activated sludge microorganisms in a two-stage continuously stirred-tank design. Results indicated that sugar and the liquid carbon source achieved the desired degree of denitrification (>99.9% removal) and the effluent selenium target concentration of <30 ppb. An overall evaluation of the use of these materials for full-scale treatment indicated that due to handling issues, the liquid carbon source was preferred over the granular sugar. This paper will discuss the results and provide more details on the implications of using these carbon sources for full-scale treatment.
KEY_FINDINGS: Results indicated that the granular sugar carbon source and the liquid carbon source (MicroCg™) achieved the desired degree of denitrification (>99.9% removal) and the effluent selenium target concentration of <30 ppb for anaerobic treatment of FGD. An overall evaluation of the use of these materials for full-scale treatment indicated that due to handling issues, the liquid carbon source was preferred over the granular sugar carbon source.
MOTIVATION: To evaluate and compare the performance of the granular sugar carbon source and the liquid carbon source in anaerobic treatment of FGD wastewaters for the biological removal of heavy metals.
MAINPARAMETER: Heavy metals (e.g., selenium, chromium, vanadium), Nitrogen

AUTHORS: Emmanuel Quagraine
TITLE: Organic Removal with Granular Activated Carbon (GAC) from Distillate Water with Bio-Fouling Tendency, and associated issues: A Follow-up Report on a Power Plant Case-Study
ABSTRACT: At IWC-2009, results of a case study evaluating organic removal options for a zero liquid discharge power plant was presented [IWC-09-27] and subsequently published in Power Plant Chemistry [2010, 12(1), 22]. For the conditions at this site, GAC was best suited and was hypothesized that the mechanism of organic removal was via mainly adsorption at the early stages of operation, but dominated by biodegradation of organics as GAC bed ages. With this notion, two GAC beds previously operated in parallel were switched to series to take advantage of organic removal via biological degradation with the upstream bed, whilst reducing excessive microbial growth on the downstream bed-the principle of biological activated carbon (BAC). It is over 2-years now that the beds were run in series and this report is to provide an update of performance since and provide evidence to support the mechanisms of organic removal from the distillate water. Discussions will include; evaluation of organic removal data (TOC, HAAs and THMs), changes in bacteria concentrations and some physicochemical parameters such as pH, and potential changes in silica and other inorganic species concentrations across the two GAC beds in series at the early and later stages of operations. The effect of backwashing and bed idling on the GAC-BAC performance is also discussed.
KEY_FINDINGS: Operating two granular activated carbon (GAC) beds in series rather than parallel changed the dynamics of the system by treating organic constituents in the first GAC bed, while reducing excessive microbial growth in the second GAC bed. After approximately 2.5 years of operation, the average TOC removal was 34% and 26% in the upstream and downstream beds, respectively. In addition, the results of the study showed that the increase in silica removal correlated with a higher contact time in the beds and that backwash and bed idling influenced the amount of inorganic ions released into the effluent.
MOTIVATION: To reduce TOC and the accumulation of "slime" or biofilm in the downstream treatment units while treating waters high in natural organic matter.
MOTIVATIONCATEGORY: Effluent limit, Water reuse, Zero liquid discharge
MAINPARAMETER: TOC, dibromoaceteic acid, chlorobromoacetic acid, trichloroacetic acid, total haloacetic acid, chloroform, pH, silica, chlorides, sodium, dissolved oxygen, temperature, turbidity, conductivity, plate count

AUTHORS: Alan Knapp, Slava Libman
TITLE: In Search of the Highest Purity Ion Exchange Resin Available Stretching the Limit of Microelectronics
ABSTRACT: The contamination levels of such common impurities as sodium, TOC (Total Organic Carbon), Silica and Boron continue to be driven down to detection limits. As micro-circuitry is measured in the nanoscale the need for ever purer deionized water is increasing with increasing complexity for the device. This paper reviews recent data compiled to evaluate resins used in the Microelectronics Industry via parameters such as rinse time and baseline impurity levels. In addition, recent resin product developments to support the Semiconductor Industry’s ITRS (International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductor) are being considered. Analytical experiments have been conducted to verify the contribution of the contamination by IX (ion exchange) resin. Different types of IX resin from leading world manufacturers have been compared for their purity. The tests included organics leach-out using both static leach and dynamic resin leach conditions. Particles SEM (Scanning Electron Microscope) analysis provide comparative results of the particles leaching from different types of resin, as well. The conducted experiment provides a technical insight for using ion exchange resin in polish mixed bed applications and consideration to quality requirements. The results of this work demonstrate the importance of different methods or the UPW Polish resin manufacturing, treatment, and handling methods. This also demonstrates the importance of the experimental examination of the IX resin used for critical applications. The ability to reuse these high quality resins in downgraded uses or less critical applications is being discussed in keeping with sustainability initiatives.
KEY_FINDINGS: Experimental analyses of different types of resin for ultrapure water/ion exchange treatment systems were designed to evaluate optimal performance for the semiconductor industry. The results of the tests performed indicate a wide range of the different resins characteristics for the four samples tested. There was no single resin that indicated the optimal performance (including which contaminants, capacity, etc.).
MOTIVATION: To evaluate the efficiency of different types of resins in treating common impurities that can disrupt semiconductor manufacturing facilities.

AUTHORS: Joon Min, Daeik Kim, Yong Eum, Gi T. Park, Sang W. Kim, Jang K.  Kim, Dae H. Rhu
TITLE: Anti-Fouling Membrane System for Industrial Wastewater Treatment and Recovery
ABSTRACT: One of the main challenges of implementing membrane technology for the industrial wastewater is fouling. An anti-fouling membrane system was developed to address these issues. This membrane system has been in full-scale operation for anaerobic digester effluent for biogas plant, methylcellulose treatment, and livestock waste treatment. The technology has also been tested in dozens of industrial and commercial sites including used motor oil waste treatment, nano silver recovery, beer fermentation process recovery, landfill leachate treatment, food waste treatment, latex manufacturing wastewater treatment, algae biomass harvesting for biogas production, wine stillage waste, or any application where conventional membranes cannot be used. This anti-fouling mechanism is based on vortex generated with uniquely designed blade between flat membrane surfaces. This system can use any membrane material including MF (micro filtration), UF (ultra filtration), or NF (nano filtration) from various suppliers. In 2004, development of a reliable anti-fouling membrane system carried out for methylcellulose wastewater from Samsung Fine Chemicals (SFC) manufacturing facility, where previous treatment systems failed due to high viscosity and high solids loading in feedwater. However, methylcellulose was recovered through this anti-fouling system. In 2009, 3 full-scale units were also installed in Netherlands to treat anaerobic digester effluent at a biogas plant owned by Mosch Thermische Installaties (MTI), where anti-fouling membrane system improved the biogas generation rate by 30% and increased stability of digester operation. Brewery process water was treated with anti-fouling membrane system to concentrate this water approximately up to 15% to sell it as an animal feedstock. These case studies and background on the anti-fouling membrane system is presented in this article.
KEY_FINDINGS: A proprietary anti-fouling membrane system incorporates membrane stacks and vortex generators to help prevent the buildup of solids on membrane filters, rendering them less effective. Each membrane module incorporates a vortex generating blade, which helps keep biosolids away from the membrane. The modular design allows for up to 20 membranes per full-scale unit stack. Three case studies (one pilot and two field studies) have implemented the anti-fouling mechanisms and results indicate that the system is highly effective at optimizing membrane performance for high viscosity, high density, and high turbidity waters in a variety of industries. However, true treatment efficiency is dependent on the membrane itself, rather than the structure of the unit around it.
MOTIVATION: To evaluate three anti-fouling technologies that can assist treatment facilities in minimizing the negative effects of fouling and help in the timely recovery of useful solids (e.g., biosolids for digester). Fouling of membrane units can shorten the lifespan of membranes, slow the treatment time of membrane units, and increase cost for chemicals and labor involved in treating membrane.

AUTHORS: Unknown
TITLE: Turnkey Treatment System Tackles Food-Processing Wastewater
ABSTRACT: In the fall of 2004, Mizkan Americas production facility in Crossville, TN, was mandated by the local authorities to pre-treat its wastewater for the reduction of BOD and TSS to less than 1,000 mg/L. As a result, John Prahler, Director of Corporate Engineering for Mizkan Americas, conducted an in-depth study to identify compact biological wastewater treatment systems that were easy to operate, required minimal maintenance, and were capable of handling fluctuating load conditions.
KEY_FINDINGS: A mustard and vinegar product processing plant installed a new comprehensive biological wastewater treatment system to treat the high-TSS and high-BOD acidic loads. The treatment system achieved TSS and BOD concentrations below 1,000 mg/L (the pre-treatment limit).
MOTIVATION: To evaluate a treatment system that can effectively reduce BOD and TSS concentrations to less than 1,000 mg/L, as mandated by local Tennessee authorities.

AUTHORS: Juzer Jangbarwala
TITLE: Transforming CBM Produced Water into a Valuable Resource
ABSTRACT:
Recently, a new fixed bed dynamic flow ion exchange system specifically designed for signature characteristics of coal bed methane (CBM) water was deployed in Wyoming's Powder River Basin. It has dramatically reduced the waste stream to less than 1% of treated water volume and has proven its economic viability.

With appropriate customized treatment, the produced water - a limiting factor in CBM capture as an energy source - becomes a valuable, environmentally friendly resource. With the waste stream minimized into a reusable form, disposal costs are eliminated and the byproduct becomes a source of revenue. Overall, the net cost reduction makes CBM production a viable form of domestic energy, and yields a much needed source of safe, usable water.
KEY_FINDINGS: The installation of a new fixed bed dynamic flow ion exchange at a coal bed methane (CBM) facility in Wyoming has proven to reduce the major contaminants of concern and eliminated liquid waste. By separating out reusable water and marketable waste byproducts, the facility has been able to effectively treat 30,000 bpd of process waste water in an arid environment.
MOTIVATION: To implement a treatment system that effectively treats CBM produced water in an arid environment suitable for irrigation or discharge into the Powder River Basin.
MOTIVATIONCATEGORY: Effluent limit, Water reuse, Zero liquid discharge

AUTHORS: Bob Kimball, Ken Klinko
TITLE: High Recovery Reverse Osmosis for Treatment of Produced Water
ABSTRACT: The CDM high-recovery RO treatment process is a pilot-tested and proven treatment system that is adaptable and cost-effective for the treatment of a wide range of gas field-produced waters. The RO process requires very little chemical addition and produces a minimal brine stream requiring off-site disposal. Based on the success of the pilot-scale testing, a full-scale system has been designed and is being constructed for treatment of 1,000 gpm coal bed methane produced water. Startup is expected in Spring 2011.
KEY_FINDINGS: CDM has developed a patent-pending process for the treatment of coal bed methane produced water in the Powder River Basin. The technology includes the following in sequence: advanced filtration, ion exchange, UV oxidation, low-pressure RO, high-pressure RO, and evaporation that are arranged to optimize water recovery and minimize chemical addition. The pilot study conducted by CDM successfully treated 500,000 gallons of feed and 3.5 million gallons of water with a 98% and 97% recovery, respectively. In addition, the pilot-scale system achieved TDS concentrations less than 500 mg/L and CaCO3 concentrations less than 5 mg/L.
MOTIVATION: To verify the necessary treatment steps to maximize overall water recovery, evaluate membrane fouling potential, and develop the necessary information for full-scale design.
MOTIVATIONCATEGORY: Effluent limit, Cost savings, Water reuse
